title: A study of novel imaging to measure scarring in chronic liver disease
official: Investigation of FAPI PET-MR for the study of fibrosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
summary:
Background and study aims
Liver scarring (fibrosis) is difficult to measure accurately. The most detailed information comes from a biopsy, but this only samples a tiny section of the liver and carries a risk of bleeding. Other techniques, such as imaging scans, are not reliably able to detect early fibrosis, subtle changes in fibrosis levels or how active the fibrosis is. This study uses a positron emission tomography magnetic resonance (PET-MR) scan with an injected tracer called fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI). The study looks at whether FAPI PET-MR can give more detail about the stage of liver fibrosis in people with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), the most common form of chronic liver disease.

Who can participate?
- Adults from the age of 40 years with a diagnosis of MASLD
- Healthy volunteers from the age of 40 years

What does the study involve?
All participants will provide background clinical information and have blood and urine samples collected. They will have an initial magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) scan, and then a FAPI PET-MR scan. The results will be compared between healthy volunteers and participants with MASLD.

A small number of participants will be asked to return for repeat MRE and FAPI PET-MR scans within 1 month to check that the scan results are consistent.

For participants with MASLD, updated clinical information about their liver disease will be collected 3 years after their initial scan. This will be used to see whether the FAPI PET-MR scan can help to predict whether liver disease is going to progress.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no direct benefits to participants taking part in this study, but the results from this study might help to improve the healthcare of patients in the future. The MRI scans undertaken in this study may provide additional information that is useful to participants' clinicians on top of their routine care.

This study requires exposures to ionising radiation. Ionising radiation can cause cancer which manifests itself after many years or decades. The risk of developing cancer as a consequence of taking part in this study is 0.01% if having one scan or 0.02% if having two scans, which is low. For comparison, the natural lifetime cancer incidence in the general population is about 50%. 

The most important potential risk is of an allergic reaction to the tracer. This is very rare (serious allergic reactions occur in approximately 1 in 10,000 participants) and there are clear procedures for managing such reactions. 

Where is the study run from?
The University of Edinburgh and NHS Lothian (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2024 to July 2029

Who is funding the study?
Investigator initiated and funded 

Who is the main contact?
Dr Christopher Box, cbox@ed.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Male or female over the age of 40 years
2. Provision of informed consent prior to any study specific procedures
Exclusion criteria:
1. Inability or unwilling to give informed consent
2. Unable to tolerate the supine position
3. Impaired renal function with eGFR of <30 mL/min/1.73 m²
4. Severe or significant comorbidity, limiting ability to undergo study procedures
5. Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding 
6. Contraindication to liver MRI (e.g. metallic implant or severe claustrophobia)
